evidence_quotes.quote: In the study, findings show that only 35% of Harijan households have access to clean water, while 85% live in crowded one-room dwellings with shared sanitation facilities, with rooms measuring 10 x 10 feet.

The research findings reveal three interconnected barriers to inclusion: (i) institutionalized job discrimination (based on temporary wages) in the municipal/corporation sanitation sector, (ii) the deliberate neglect of Harijan settlements in urban planning, which is evident in the research, and (iii) social exclusion that perpetuates poverty across generations.

Although the city corporation deducts payments for utilities from worker salaries directly, residents were never issued official utility bills in their names. As a result there is little documentation, which makes it difficult to go through formal processes, such as applying for a passport, as police verification often requires proof of being a utility holder.

Based on a six-month mixed-methods field study (March-August 2023), the study included household surveys (n=150), in-depth interviews (n=30), focus group discussions, participant observation and case study to reveal patterns of exclusion related to housing, water access, employment, and education.
Water access remains inadequate. Only 35% of households have piped water access, compared to the national average of 85%

criterion_notes.c1: Yes. Although most mentions of 'sanitation' in the paper refer to municipal sanitation labor (sweeping/cleaning jobs), the paper also examines household water and sanitation service conditions in Ganakatuli Sweeper Colony, reporting household piped/clean water access (35% vs. 85% national average) and shared sanitation facilities (85% living in crowded one-room dwellings with shared sanitation facilities).
criterion_notes.c2: No. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper broadly discusses institutional, legal, and governance themes—specifically constitutional equality gaps under Articles 27 and 28, general neglect of Harijan colonies in urban planning (unfulfilled 2018 housing rehabilitation promises and ignored requests for a boundary wall), circumvention of an 80% Harijan quota in municipal sanitation employment, and municipal payroll deductions for generic utilities without issuing official utility bills in residents' names. However, even under the plain reading, those institutional mechanisms are analyzed in relation to sanitation employment, housing/security, school enrollment, and passport police verification rather than household water or sanitation service access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification (requiring a rule-type mechanism—eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure—directly governing water or sanitation service access, rather than generic project delivery or unanalysed macro-governance background), Criterion 2 is clearly not met: the 35% piped water access rate and 85% shared sanitation rate are presented solely as descriptive colony-level SDG living-condition deficits attributed to broad caste marginalization and unanalysed macro-governance/urban-planning neglect, while the municipal payroll utility-deduction practice (not issuing individual utility bills) is analyzed only as creating a documentation barrier to passport verification, not as governing water or sanitation access.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Contains primary empirical evidence from a six-month mixed-methods field study (March–August 2023) in Ganakatuli Sweeper Colony, Dhaka, combining structured household surveys, in-depth interviews (n=30), focus group discussions, and participant observation.
criterion_notes.c4: Yes. Reports descriptive colony-level access outcomes: 35% of households have piped/clean water access (a 50 percentage-point deficit compared to the 85% national average) and 85% live in one-room dwellings with shared sanitation facilities.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. The study identifies the population and unit of analysis (households and residents in Ganakatuli Sweeper Colony, Dhaka), broad exposure (caste/religious status and socio-spatial institutional neglect of a sweeper colony), descriptive outcomes (including piped water access and shared sanitation alongside income, literacy, housing space, and employment), and a mixed-methods case-study design. Note internal reporting inconsistencies in sample counts (text states n=150 household surveys and 3 or 5 FGDs, whereas Tables 1–2 report n=1,494 households / 8,867 individuals) and that piped water access (35%) is reported only as a single colony-wide figure without linkage to any water-specific legal or administrative rule.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English (note: retrieved PDF is the 2025 Research Square preprint version, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-6596476/v1, matching the record title and core authors).

study_design: Mixed-methods cross-sectional case study (household survey, in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, and participant observation)
population_and_sample: Households and residents (Hindu Harijans and Muslim Cleaners) in Ganakatuli Sweeper Colony, Dhaka, Bangladesh; text reports n=150 household surveys, n=30 in-depth interviews, and 3 (or 5) focus group discussions, while Tables 1-2 report n=1,494 households (8,867 individuals)
exposure: Caste-based socio-spatial marginalization, occupational discrimination in municipal sanitation employment, and general institutional/urban-planning neglect (no rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation service access)
outcome: Descriptive colony-level household piped water access (35% vs. 85% national average; 50% water access deficit) and shared sanitation facilities (85% living in one-room dwellings with shared sanitation), alongside income, literacy, school dropout, housing space, and sanitation-sector employment
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). The retrieved full text (the Research Square preprint of the matching paper) empirically documents living and working conditions in Ganakatuli Sweeper Colony in Dhaka, including descriptive statistics that 35% of households have piped/clean water access and 85% share sanitation facilities. However, it fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 clarification because it does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, eligibility, tenure, or tariff mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. Most analysis of 'sanitation' concerns employment discrimination and quota circumvention in municipal sweeper jobs; water and sanitation access deficits are treated solely as descriptive SDG indicators reflecting broad caste marginalization and unanalysed macro-governance/urban-planning neglect, while the lack of individual utility bills (despite municipal salary deductions) is examined only as a documentation barrier to passport police verification rather than a mechanism governing water or sanitation service access.
